items.stem:
A perfectly competitive firm's total revenue schedule is:
Output | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6
TR (₹) | 0 | 12 | 24 | 36 | 48 | 60 | 72
Find the MR at 3 units.
items.markingKey: MR = TR(3) − TR(2) = 36 − 24 = 12. Under perfect competition AR = MR = price.

items.stem:

items.markingKey: MR = TR(3) − TR(2) = 45 − 30 = 15. Under perfect competition AR = MR = price.

items.markingKey: AR = TR/q = 32/4 = 8. Under perfect competition AR = MR = price.

items.stem:
Tanvi sells wheat in a perfectly competitive market where the price is ₹6 per kg.
(i) Find TR from selling 8 kg.
(ii) What are AR and MR at 8 kg?
(iii) What is the shape of the TR curve?
(iv) Can Tanvi sell more by lowering the price slightly? Why?
items.answer: (i) ₹48; (ii) AR = MR = ₹6; (iii) A straight line through the origin with slope equal to price; (iv) No need: any quantity can be sold at the market price; the firm is a price taker

items.stem: Why is a firm under perfect competition a price taker?
items.answer: Large number of firms each with a tiny share; homogeneous product; perfect knowledge; so price is set by market demand and supply.

items.stem: The TR curve of a perfectly competitive firm is
items.answer: an upward sloping straight line from the origin
options: an upward sloping straight line from the origin
an inverted U-shaped curve
a rectangular hyperbola
a horizontal line

TR (₹) | 0 | 20 | 40 | 60 | 80 | 100 | 120
Find the AR at 3 units.
items.markingKey: AR = TR/q = 60/3 = 20. Under perfect competition AR = MR = price.

items.stem: Explain the features of perfect competition and show the shapes of TR, AR and MR curves of a firm in such a market.
items.answer: Features: many buyers and sellers, homogeneous product, free entry/exit, perfect knowledge, perfect mobility; TR straight line from origin, AR = MR horizontal at market price.

items.answer: 7 units; profit = ₹10
items.markingKey: MC: 19, 14, 11, 16, 18, 20, 23. p = MC = 23 at 7 units with MC rising (and p ≥ AVC = 17.29). TR = 161, TC = 151 → profit 10. (Unit 7 adds nothing to profit, so profit at 6 units is the same; by the rule p = MC the answer is 7 units.)

TC (₹) | 30 | 46 | 57 | 66 | 78 | 96 | 120 | 146
(i) Calculate MC at each output.
(ii) At what output is profit maximum? State the conditions used.
(iii) Calculate TR and profit at that output.
(iv) Why will the firm not produce one more unit?
items.answer: (i) 16, 11, 9, 12, 18, 24, 26; (ii) 7 units: p = MC and MC rising; (iii) TR = ₹182; profit = ₹36; (iv) MC of the next unit (higher) exceeds the price

items.stem: Why must MC be rising at the profit-maximising output?
items.answer: If MC is falling where p = MC, producing a little more makes p > MC, adding to profit; so that point is not the maximum.

(ii) Find the profit-maximising output, stating both conditions.
(iii) Calculate the profit or loss at that output.

items.answer: (i) TFC = ₹20; MC: 12, 9, 6, 10, 15, 19, 22; (ii) 5 units (p = MC = 15, MC rising); (iii) Profit = ₹3 (TR 75 − TC 72); (iv) Minimum AVC = 9; p = 15 ≥ min AVC, so it continues

items.stem: Explain the equilibrium of a perfectly competitive firm using the MR–MC approach with a diagram.

items.markingKey: 2 marks conditions; 2 marks diagram; 2 marks explanation (6 marks).

items.stem: A firm in a perfectly competitive market sells at ₹5 per unit. Find its total revenue from 5 units, and its AR and MR.
items.answer: TR = ₹25; AR = MR = ₹5
items.markingKey: TR = p × q = 5 × 5 = 25; AR = TR/q = 5; MR = ΔTR = 5.

items.stem: For a perfectly competitive firm, minimum AVC = ₹22 and minimum AC = ₹30. If the market price is ₹28, in the short run the firm will
items.answer: Produce at a loss in the short run
items.markingKey: (b) min AVC < p < min AC: variable cost covered, part of fixed cost lost.
